intro: Couples, weddings, children, and how to talk about the way kids behave.
p.pareja.consejo: It is feminine even when it refers to a man: «mi pareja». It works for partners and spouses.
p.boda.consejo: You say «ir a una boda». The verb is «casarse» and the stars are «los novios».
p.luna de miel.consejo: As in English, it has «luna» (moon) and «miel» (honey). It takes «de»: «irse de luna de miel».
p.separarse.consejo: It is reflexive: «se separan». After separating, a divorce may follow.
p.divorcio.consejo: The verb is «divorciarse». For the beginning you say «casarse».
p.adoptar.consejo: It also works for ideas and habits: «adoptar una buena actitud».
p.educar.consejo: «Educar» is not only teaching at school: it is also bringing up a child at home.
p.obedecer.consejo: In the «yo» form it has zc: «obedezco». The opposite is «desobedecer».
p.portarse bien.consejo: It is used a lot with children: «pórtate bien». The opposite is «portarse mal».
p.travieso.consejo: It is said with affection. «Maleducado» is a much more serious criticism.
p.guardería.consejo: It comes from «guardar» (to keep): children are looked after there while their parents work.
p.canguro.consejo: It is also the Australian animal. For the person, both «el canguro» and «la canguro» work.
p.infancia.consejo: It comes from «infante», a small child. You say «en mi infancia».
b1.texto:
Today we talk about couples, families and children.

- **Couples:** two people can **casarse** (get married, with a **boda**) and then go on a **luna de miel**. If the relationship ends, they **se separan** and, later, there may be a **divorcio**.
- **Children:** parents can **adoptar** a child. You say **educar** a son or daughter. The youngest go to the **guardería**, and at night a **canguro** can look after them.
- **Behaviour:** a child can **portarse bien** and **obedecer** their parents. A child who plays small pranks is **travieso**; one who is disrespectful is **maleducado**.
- **Careful:** **educado** means «polite and courteous», not «with an education».
- **Time together:** **llevar** + time: llevan diez años juntos (they have been together for ten years).
b2.f0.texto: My brother is getting married in June.
b2.f1.texto: Is it going to be a big wedding?
b2.f2.texto: They want a small party and a quiet honeymoon.
b2.f3.texto: Who is going to look after the children?
b2.f4.texto: My cousin works as a babysitter at weekends.
b2.f5.texto: My son is very naughty and obeys nobody.
b2.f6.texto: With my cousin he always behaves well.
b2.f7.texto: That way we can dance in peace.
b4.texto:
To say **for how long** something has lasted, Spanish uses **llevar** + time:

- **llevar** + time + adjective or adverb: **llevan diez años juntos** (they have been together for ten years).
- **llevar** + time + gerund: **llevo dos años viviendo aquí** (I have been living here for two years).

The verb **llevar** changes with the person (llevo, llevas, lleva, llevamos, lleváis, llevan); the time it counts does not. It is a very natural way to talk about couples, jobs and habits.
b4.e0.texto: My parents have been married for thirty years.
b4.e1.texto: We have been living together as a couple for two years.
b4.e2.texto: My cousin has been looking for a nursery for a month.
b5.f0.texto: Rosa's house smells of soup and warm bread.
b5.f1.texto: Three generations gather around a long table.
b5.f2.texto: The grandparents have been married for fifty years and still look at each other tenderly.
b5.f3.texto: The little grandchildren run mischievously between the chairs.
b5.f4.texto: Their mother watches them from the kitchen with a tired smile.
b5.f5.texto: Rosa serves the soup and asks the children to behave.
b5.f6.texto: The little ones obey for a minute and then go back to their games.
b5.f7.texto: Grandfather remembers his childhood in a village with no nursery and no toys.
b5.f8.texto: He says that back then the children played in the street until night.
b5.f9.texto: At the end of the afternoon, everyone clears the table and says goodbye with a hug.
b6.o0.refuerzo: Yes! «Educado» is about good manners, not studies.
b6.o1.refuerzo: For that you say «culto» or «con estudios». «Educado» is something else.
b6.o2.refuerzo: A naughty child plays pranks; «educado» is about good manners.
b6.pregunta: What does «un chico muy educado» mean?
b7.o0.refuerzo: «Obedece» is for one person. Here there are several children.
b7.o2.refuerzo: The infinitive is not conjugated. The «ellos» form is needed.
b8.frase: Los niños se portan muy bien en la boda
b8.traduccion: The children behave very well at the wedding
b9.o0.refuerzo: The nursery is a place for the daytime, not at home at night.
b9.o1.refuerzo: A divorce is the end of a marriage, not a person.
b9.o2.refuerzo: Well done! The babysitter looks after the children while the parents go out.
b9.pregunta: Who looks after the children at home at night?
b11.o0.refuerzo: That's it! «Llevar» + time says how long something has lasted.
b11.o1.refuerzo: «Tener años» is about age. For time together you use «llevar».
b11.o2.refuerzo: «Estar» does not count time this way. With time plus adjective, use «llevar».
b11.pregunta: Which verb is missing to count the years?
b12.o0.refuerzo: «Maleducado» is more serious: he shows no respect for others.
b12.o1.refuerzo: That's it! «Travieso» is said fondly about pranks.
b12.o2.refuerzo: An obedient child does what he is told; he plays no pranks.
b12.pregunta: A child who plays small pranks is…
p.hijo.consejo: The j sounds like h; the feminine is «hija».
p.obedece.consejo: From «obedecer»: the c becomes z before e, so «obedece» ends in -ce.
p.casados.consejo: Plural of «casado»; it describes people who are married.
p.buscando.consejo: The gerund of «buscar» ends in «-ando», like «buscando».
p.generaciones.consejo: The plural of «generación» keeps the same sound pattern; the j-like g is a soft h.
p.reúnen.consejo: From «reunir»; the u takes the accent so the two vowels stay apart.
p.traviesos.consejo: Describes children who play pranks; the v sounds like b.
p.vigila.consejo: From «vigilar»: the g in «vigila» is a soft h.
p.porten.consejo: From «portarse»: «que se porten bien» means that they behave well.
p.obedecen.consejo: From «obedecer»: the c before e sounds like th in Spain.
p.juegos.consejo: The j sounds like h, and the g before e is soft.
p.juguetes.consejo: The j sounds like h; the u is pronounced clearly.
p.jugaban.consejo: Imperfect of «jugar»: it describes what used to happen.
p.recogen.consejo: From «recoger»: the g before e sounds like h.
p.despiden.consejo: From «despedirse»: the verb is reflexive, like «se despiden».
